question: Why does azo coupling occur predominantly at the para position relative to the activating group (-\text{OH} or -\text{NH}_2)?
options: Because the diazonium cation is a bulky electrophile, steric hindrance disfavors ortho attack, directing substitution almost exclusively to the less hindered para position
Because ortho positions are blocked by chlorine
Because meta positions are more reactive
explanation: The diazonium group is sterically demanding; unless the para position is already blocked, coupling occurs selectively at the open para position.
subject: Chemistry

question: What happens during azo coupling if the para position of the phenol is already occupied (e.g., in $p$-cresol)?
options: No reaction occurs under any condition
Coupling takes place at one of the unoccupied ortho positions to the $-\text{OH}$ group
The methyl group is displaced as methane gas
The ring opens to form an aliphatic dialdehyde
explanation: If the para position is blocked by a substituent, electrophilic attack by the diazonium ion is directed to the ortho position relative to the activating $-\text{OH}$ group.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why are azo compounds intensely colored and widely used as commercial dyes?
options: Because nitrogen atoms emit fluorescent radiation
Because of impurities in the glassware

They possess an extended conjugated system of alternating double and single bonds spanning two aromatic rings connected by the azo chromophore ($-\text{N=N}-$), which absorbs light in the visible spectrum
Because of high molecular weight alone
explanation: The azo group ($-\text{N=N}-$) serves as an excellent chromophore. Delocalization across both aromatic rings narrows the $\text{HOMO-LUMO}$ energy gap, shifting absorption into the visible spectrum.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the product when benzenediazonium chloride is coupled with $\beta$-naphthol (2-naphthol) in alkaline solution?
explanation: $\beta$-Naphthol couples exclusively at the 1-position (ortho to the 2-hydroxy group) because attack at C1 preserves the aromaticity of the other benzene ring in the Wheland intermediate.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why does $\beta$-naphthol couple exclusively at the 1-position and NEVER at the 3-position?
options: Attack at the 1-position yields a resonance-stabilized arenium ion that preserves the intact benzene sextet, whereas attack at the 3-position disrupts aromatic resonance throughout the entire bicyclic system
The 3-position is blocked by a proton that cannot be removed
The 3-position has a formal positive charge
explanation: Electrophilic attack at C1 produces 2 favorable resonance contributors with an intact benzene ring, whereas attack at C3 produces none without disrupting the second ring.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the name of the qualitative analytical test based on $\beta$-naphthol coupling used to confirm primary aromatic amines?
explanation: The amine is diazotized with $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ at $0-5^\circ\text{C}$ and poured into an alkaline solution of $\beta$-naphthol; formation of a brilliant scarlet-red dye confirms a primary aromatic amine.
subject: Chemistry

question: Can aliphatic primary amines give a positive Azo Dye Test with $\beta$-naphthol?
options: No, because aliphatic diazonium ions decompose instantaneously with loss of $\text{N}_2$ gas and never survive to couple with $\beta$-naphthol
explanation: Aliphatic diazonium ions are exceedingly unstable; they lose dinitrogen within picoseconds to form carbocations, yielding alcohols and alkenes instead of azo dyes.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the starting material and second component for the preparation of the acid-base indicator Methyl Orange?
explanation: Diazotized sulfanilic acid is coupled with $N,N$-dimethylaniline in mildly acidic aqueous solution to yield methyl orange dye.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the color change of Methyl Orange across its transition pH range ($3.1 - 4.4$)?
options: Red in acidic medium ($\text{pH } < 3.1$) to Yellow in alkaline/neutral medium ($\text{pH } > 4.4$)
Yellow in acidic to Blue in basic
Colorless in acidic to Pink in basic
Green in acidic to Orange in basic
explanation: In acidic solution, protonation occurs at the azo nitrogen, forming a quinonoid resonance contributor with a narrower $\text{HOMO-LUMO}$ gap that absorbs green light and appears red.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why does Methyl Orange turn red upon protonation in acidic solution?
options: Protonation at the azo nitrogen forms a highly delocalized quinonoid structure extending across both rings, shifting the absorption spectrum bathochromically (to longer wavelengths)
Because the molecule cleaves into two halves
Because methyl groups dissociate into methane
explanation: The quinonoid form has extensive resonance delocalization between the terminal dimethylamino group and the sulfonic acid moiety, shifting absorption from blue to green (appearing red).
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the structure of Congo Red, a classic direct dye for cotton?
options: A disazo dye formed by coupling tetrazotized benzidine with two molecules of naphthionic acid (4-amino-1-naphthalenesulfonic acid)
explanation: Congo Red contains two azo linkages ($-\text{N=N}-$) linking a central biphenyl core to two 1-amino-4-sulfonaphthalene end-groups.
subject: Chemistry

question: What happens during azo coupling when an electron-withdrawing group (such as $-\text{NO}_2$) is present on the arenediazonium ion?
options: The coupling reaction is completely inhibited
The diazonium ion turns into a nucleophile
The reaction requires a temperature above $200^\circ\text{C}$
The coupling reaction proceeds significantly faster because the electron-withdrawing group increases the positive charge density and electrophilicity of the diazonium group
explanation: $p$-Nitrobenzenediazonium ion is a substantially more potent electrophile than unsubstituted benzenediazonium ion and can even couple with reactive ethers (e.g., anisole).
subject: Chemistry

question: Which of the following diazonium ions is the most reactive electrophile in azo coupling?
explanation: Strongly electron-withdrawing nitro groups at the 2, 4, and 6 positions maximally deplete electron density from the diazonium group, rendering it a ferocious electrophile.
subject: Chemistry

question: Which of the following aromatic substrates is LEAST likely to undergo azo coupling with benzenediazonium chloride?
explanation: Nitrobenzene is strongly deactivated by the $-\text{NO}_2$ group; weak electrophiles like diazonium ions can only substitute strongly activated rings (phenols, amines).
subject: Chemistry

question: When aniline is treated with benzenediazonium chloride at $\text{pH } 7$, what intermediate is preferentially formed initially before rearrangement?
options: Diazoaminobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{N=N}-\text{NH}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$), where coupling occurred at nitrogen rather than carbon
explanation: Under neutral conditions, the diazonium electrophile attacks the amino nitrogen lone pair (kinetic control) to yield the yellow crystalline diazoaminobenzene.
subject: Chemistry

question: How is diazoaminobenzene rearranged into the thermodynamically stable $C$-coupled product ($p$-aminoazobenzene)?
options: By adding excess sodium hydroxide at $0^\circ\text{C}$
By heating with aniline hydrochloride at $40-50^\circ\text{C}$ in the presence of acid
explanation: Acid protonates diazoaminobenzene, which cleaves reversibly back into diazonium ion and aniline; the diazonium ion then attacks the para carbon of aniline irreversibly.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is an auxochrome in an azo dye molecule?
options: A functional group ($-\text{OH}$, $-\text{NH}_2$, $-\text{NR}_2$, $-\text{SO}_3\text{Na}$) that deepens the color and binds or fastens the dye to fabric fibers
The group that bleaches the dye
explanation: Auxochromes contain non-bonding lone pairs that conjugate with the $\pi$-system, shifting absorption bathochromically and conferring water solubility or fabric affinity.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is a chromophore in an azo dye?
options: The light-absorbing unsaturated group containing $\pi$-electrons, specifically the azo linkage ($-\text{N=N}-$)
explanation: Chromophores (such as $-\text{N=N}-$, $-\text{NO}_2$, $-\text{C=O}$) are structural entities responsible for selective absorption of visible light.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the product when resorcinol (benzene-1,3-diol) is coupled with benzenediazonium chloride?
options: Sudan Orange G (4-(phenyldiazenyl)benzene-1,3-diol), where substitution occurs at C4 (ortho to one -OH, para to the other)
explanation: Both hydroxyl groups reinforce activation at the 4-position (which is ortho to C3 and para to C1); C2 is heavily sterically hindered by both adjacent hydroxyls.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why is coupling at position 2 of resorcinol disfavored compared to position 4?
options: Position 2 is sterically crowded between two bulky hydroxyl groups, whereas position 4 is much less hindered
explanation: Steric hindrance between the two neighboring $-\text{OH}$ substituents prevents attack of the bulky diazonium ion at C2, directing it to position 4.
subject: Chemistry

question: What happens when an azo dye is treated with strong reducing agents such as $\text{SnCl}_2 + \text{HCl}$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_4$?
options: Reductive cleavage of the azo bond ($-\text{N=N}-$) occurs, yielding two molecules of primary aromatic amines
explanation: Reductive cleavage: $\text{Ar}-\text{N=N}-\text{Ar}' + 4[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{Ar}-\text{NH}_2 + \text{Ar}'-\text{NH}_2$. This reaction is historically used to identify the structure of azo dyes.
subject: Chemistry

question: When $p$-aminoazobenzene is reduced with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, what are the products?
explanation: Cleavage of the central azo bond delivers one molecule of aniline and one molecule of benzene-1,4-diamine ($p$-phenylenediamine).
subject: Chemistry

question: Why is butter yellow ($p$-dimethylaminoazobenzene), formerly used to color butter, banned as a food additive?
options: It is a potent liver carcinogen that causes hepatic tumors in animal models upon metabolic azo reduction and bioactivation
explanation: Azo reduction of butter yellow generates reactive carcinogenic aromatic amine metabolites; it is strictly prohibited worldwide.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is Prontosil, the first commercially available synthetic antibacterial drug discovered by Gerhard Domagk?
options: A red azo dye containing a sulfonamide group, which is metabolically cleaved in vivo into the active antibacterial agent sulfanilamide
explanation: Prontosil is a prodrug; in the mammalian body, azoreductase enzymes reduce its azo linkage to release free sulfanilamide, which inhibits bacterial folic acid synthesis.
subject: Chemistry

question: In which medium does $\alpha$-naphthol (1-naphthol) undergo azo coupling with benzenediazonium ion?
options: Predominantly at the 4-position in alkaline solution
explanation: $\alpha$-Naphthol couples mainly at position 4 (para to $-\text{OH}$); if position 4 is blocked, coupling takes place at position 2.
subject: Chemistry

question: What type of isomerism is exhibited by azo compounds containing the $-\text{N=N}-$ linkage?
explanation: Due to restricted rotation about the nitrogen-nitrogen double bond, azo compounds exist as trans (E) and cis (Z) isomers; the trans isomer is thermodynamically much more stable.
subject: Chemistry

question: What happens when trans-azobenzene is exposed to ultraviolet light ($\text{UV}$)?
options: It breaks into two molecules of benzene
It undergoes reversible photoisomerization to cis-azobenzene, changing its absorption spectrum and dipole moment
explanation: Azobenzene is a prototypical molecular photoswitch: $\text{UV}$ light drives trans-to-cis isomerization, while visible light or heat reverses it back to trans.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the geometry around each nitrogen atom in trans-azobenzene ($\text{Ph-N=N-Ph}$)?
options: Bent with approximately $120^\circ$ bond angles ($\text{sp}^2$ hybridized)
explanation: Each nitrogen in the $-\text{N=N}-$ group is $\text{sp}^2$ hybridized, having one single bond to carbon, one double bond to nitrogen, and one lone pair, yielding a bent geometry.
subject: Chemistry

question: Which of the following compounds CANNOT undergo azo coupling with benzenediazonium chloride?
explanation: Toluene contains only a weakly activating alkyl group ($+I$, hyperconjugation), which is insufficient to activate the ring for attack by the weak diazonium electrophile.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the effect of an electron-donating substituent (such as $-\text{OCH}_3$) on the diazonium ion during coupling?
options: It speeds up coupling by $1000$ times
It decreases the positive charge on the diazonium nitrogen, drastically lowering its electrophilicity and slowing down the coupling reaction
It converts the diazonium salt into an alkane
It makes coupling independent of pH
explanation: Electron donation stabilizes the diazonium cation through resonance, diminishing its electrophilic character and reactivity toward coupling substrates.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why is the reaction temperature strictly maintained at $0-5^\circ\text{C}$ during azo coupling?
options: To keep the azo dye in liquid state
To prevent freezing of the water
To prevent thermal hydrolysis of the arenediazonium salt into phenol and evolution of nitrogen gas
To maximize the speed of light absorption
explanation: Diazonium ions hydrolyze rapidly at temperatures above $5-10^\circ\text{C}$; maintaining an ice-cold temperature ensures that the diazonium ion remains intact to couple cleanly.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the role of sodium acetate in azo coupling with amines?
options: It serves as the main oxidizing agent
It bleaches the color of the dye
It acts as a buffer to maintain the $\text{pH}$ around $4-5$, neutralizing the $\text{HCl}$ liberated during the reaction without making the solution strongly basic
explanation: As coupling proceeds, $\text{HCl}$ is generated: $\text{ArN}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{Ar}'\text{NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ar}-\text{N=N}-\text{Ar}'\text{NH}_2 + \text{HCl}$. Sodium acetate buffers the reaction so acidity does not rise to the point of deactivating the amine.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why does azo coupling of benzenediazonium ion with pyrrole occur readily without a catalyst?
options: Pyrrole is an exceedingly electron-rich, $\pi$-excessive heteroaromatic ring that reacts readily even with weak electrophiles
Pyrrole contains a strong mineral acid
explanation: Pyrrole possesses 6 $\pi$-electrons distributed over only 5 ring atoms, giving it very high electron density; it couples smoothly with diazonium ions at position 2.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is Tartrazine (FD&C Yellow 5), widely used in foods and cosmetics?
options: A synthetic yellow azo dye containing pyrazole and sulfonate rings
explanation: Tartrazine is a water-soluble pyrazolone azo dye synthesized via azo coupling chemistry, commonly added to candies, soft drinks, and seasonings.
subject: Chemistry

question: What test distinguishes 1-naphthol from 2-naphthol using diazotized sulfanilic acid?
options: 1-Naphthol couples at the 4-position giving a reddish-brown dye, whereas 2-naphthol couples at the 1-position giving a bright red/scarlet crystalline dye with different chromatographic mobility
explanation: Both undergo coupling at different positions (C4 vs C1), producing distinct azo dyes with different shades, melting points, and spectral characteristics.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the intermediate formed during the electrophilic attack of benzenediazonium ion on phenoxide ion?
options: A resonance-stabilized $\sigma$-complex (Wheland intermediate) containing a cyclohexadienone core before losing a proton
explanation: Electrophilic attack by $[\text{Ar}-\text{N}_2]^+$ at the para position of phenoxide forms a cyclohexadienone $\sigma$-complex that rapidly loses a proton to re-aromatize into the azo phenoxide.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the overall reaction classification for azo coupling in dyes manufacturing?
options: Carbon-nitrogen bond-forming electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction
explanation: Azo coupling creates a new $\text{C-N}$ covalent bond between an aromatic ring carbon of the nucleophilic substrate and the terminal nitrogen of the diazonium cation.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the Sandmeyer reaction in organic synthesis?
options: The replacement of the diazonium group ($-\text{N}_2^+$) in an arenediazonium salt by $-\text{Cl}$, $-\text{Br}$, or $-\text{CN}$ using copper(I) salts as catalysts
The reduction of nitrobenzene to aniline using tin and hydrochloric acid
The conversion of an amide to a primary amine with bromine and alkali
The coupling of two aryl halides with sodium metal in dry ether
explanation: Discovered by Traugott Sandmeyer in 1884, the Sandmeyer reaction uses cuprous salts ($\text{CuCl}$, $\text{CuBr}$, or $\text{CuCN}$) to substitute the diazonium moiety with chloro, bromo, or cyano groups.
subject: Chemistry

question: What catalyst is typically employed in the Sandmeyer reaction to introduce a chlorine atom onto an aromatic ring?
options: Copper(I) chloride dissolved in concentrated hydrochloric acid ($\text{CuCl} / \text{HCl}$)
explanation: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{CuCl}/\text{HCl}} \text{Ar-Cl} + \text{N}_2\uparrow$. $\text{CuCl}$ acts as a single-electron transfer catalyst.
subject: Chemistry

question: Which reagents are used in the Sandmeyer reaction to prepare benzonitrile from benzenediazonium chloride?
explanation: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}} \text{Ar-CN} + \text{N}_2\uparrow$. This is a crucial method for forming aryl $\text{C-C}$ bonds.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the accepted mechanism for the Sandmeyer reaction?
options: An electrophilic aromatic substitution via a carbocation intermediate
A radical-nucleophilic process initiated by Single Electron Transfer (SET) from copper(I) to the diazonium cation, generating an aryl radical ($\text{Ar}^\bullet$) and copper(II)
explanation: Mechanism: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+ + \text{Cu}^\text{I}\text{X} \rightarrow \text{Ar}^\bullet + \text{N}_2 + \text{Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}^+$. Then $\text{Ar}^\bullet + \text{Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ar-X} + \text{Cu}^\text{I}\text{X}$.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the role of copper(I) in the catalytic cycle of the Sandmeyer reaction?
options: It acts as a one-electron reducing agent that transfers an electron to the diazonium cation and subsequently transfers the halogen/pseudohalogen back to the aryl radical
It acts as a Lewis acid to cleave the benzene ring
It acts as an oxidizing agent that consumes nitrogen
It absorbs water molecules from the reaction solvent
explanation: Copper alternates between $\text{Cu}^\text{I}$ and $\text{Cu}^\text{II}$ oxidation states, facilitating single-electron reduction to create the aryl radical and then ligand transfer to complete substitution.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why is copper(I) catalyst NOT required for the preparation of iodobenzene from benzenediazonium chloride?
options: Iodine gas decomposes the diazonium salt spontaneously
Iodide ion ($\text{I}^-$) is a sufficiently powerful reducing agent to directly transfer an electron to the diazonium cation without needing a transition metal catalyst
Iodine is a gas and does not dissolve in water
Copper iodide explodes violently with diazonium salts
explanation: $\text{I}^-$ has a low oxidation potential (easily oxidized to $\text{I}_2$). Simple warming of the aqueous diazonium solution with $\text{KI}$ affords iodobenzene in high yield: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{KI} \rightarrow \text{Ar-I} + \text{KCl} + \text{N}_2\uparrow$.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why can fluorobenzene NOT be prepared using the classic Sandmeyer reaction with copper(I) fluoride ($\text{CuF}$)?
options: Fluorine burns the benzene ring to ashes
Fluorobenzene is unstable and decomposes into acetylene
Fluoride ion has high hydration energy, high oxidation potential, and forms insoluble inactive copper fluorides; fluorobenzene is instead prepared via the Balz-Schiemann reaction using $\text{HBF}_4$
Diazonium ions reject all halogens except iodine
explanation: The copper(I)/copper(II) redox cycle does not operate effectively with fluoride ligands. Heating diazonium fluoroborate ($\text{ArN}_2^+\text{BF}_4^-$) is used instead (Balz-Schiemann reaction).
subject: Chemistry

question: How does the Gattermann reaction differ from the Sandmeyer reaction?
options: The Gattermann reaction uses iron powder instead of copper
The Gattermann reaction prepares only aliphatic amines
The Gattermann reaction requires liquid ammonia
The Gattermann reaction uses finely divided copper powder with $\text{HX}$ instead of cuprous halide ($\text{Cu}_2\text{X}_2 / \text{HX}$)
explanation: In the Gattermann reaction: $\text{ArN}_2^+\text{X}^- \xrightarrow{\text{Cu powder}/\text{HX}} \text{Ar-X} + \text{N}_2 + \text{CuX}$. It gives slightly lower yields (~40%) than the Sandmeyer reaction (~70-80%).
subject: Chemistry

question: Between the Sandmeyer reaction and the Gattermann reaction, which generally provides superior yields and purity of aryl halides?
options: The Sandmeyer reaction gives substantially higher yields and fewer side products because copper(I) halides dissolve to form active homogeneous halocuprate complexes
The Gattermann reaction gives $100\%$ yield while Sandmeyer gives zero
Both reactions give identical yields of less than $5\%$
explanation: Sandmeyer's use of cuprous halides ($\text{CuX}$) provides higher yields (~70–80%) compared to Gattermann's heterogeneous copper powder method (~40%).
subject: Chemistry

question: What gas is quantitatively evolved as a thermodynamic driving force in the Sandmeyer reaction?
explanation: The formation of the exceptionally stable $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond ($\sim 945\text{ kJ/mol}$ bond enthalpy) provides an enormous thermodynamic driving force (entropy increase and large exothermicity).
subject: Chemistry

question: What common side product is formed via dimerization of two aryl radicals during the Sandmeyer reaction?
explanation: When two free aryl radicals encounter each other before halogen transfer from $\text{Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}_2$, radical combination produces symmetrical biaryls: $2\text{Ar}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{Ar-Ar}$.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why is the Sandmeyer reaction preferred over direct electrophilic aromatic halogenation for preparing $o$-chlorotoluene from toluene?
options: Direct chlorination of toluene destroys the benzene ring
Toluene cannot react with chlorine in the presence of $\text{FeCl}_3$

Direct chlorination of toluene produces an inseparable mixture of ortho and para isomers, whereas nitration followed by isomer separation, reduction, diazotization, and Sandmeyer reaction yields pure $o$-chlorotoluene
explanation: The Sandmeyer pathway allows regiospecific synthesis of pure single positional isomers (such as $o$-chlorotoluene or $m$-bromotoluene) that cannot be obtained purely by direct electrophilic halogenation.
subject: Chemistry

question: How can $m$-bromotoluene be synthesized from toluene, given that the methyl group is ortho/para-directing?
options: Nitrate toluene $\rightarrow$ separate $p$-nitrotoluene $\rightarrow$ brominate meta to methyl (ortho to nitro) $\rightarrow$ reduce $-\text{NO}_2$ to $-\text{NH}_2$ $\rightarrow$ diazotize $\rightarrow$ deaminate with $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2$
explanation: Strategic use of the amino/diazonium handle allows removal or replacement at specific positions to generate products inaccessible by direct substitution.
subject: Chemistry

question: What safety precaution must be taken when performing the Sandmeyer cyanation reaction with $\text{CuCN}$?
options: The reaction must be carried out in pure oxygen

The acidic diazonium solution must be neutralized with sodium carbonate before adding the copper(I) cyanide-potassium cyanide complex to prevent evolution of deadly hydrogen cyanide ($\text{HCN}$) gas
The mixture must be heated with an open flame
Liquid sodium must be poured into the flask
explanation: Acidic solutions decompose cyanide salts into lethal volatile $\text{HCN}$ gas: $\text{CN}^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{HCN}\uparrow$. Thus, neutralization to neutral or mildly alkaline pH is mandatory.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the synthetic utility of converting an arenediazonium salt into a benzonitrile via Sandmeyer cyanation?
options: Nitriles cannot undergo any further reactions
The nitrile group always falls off as carbon monoxide

The nitrile group ($-\text{CN}$) introduces a new carbon atom and can be readily hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$), reduced to a primary benzylamine ($-\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$), or converted to an aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$)
It is only useful for making plastic explosives
explanation: Sandmeyer cyanation is one of the most powerful methods for building benzoic acids, aryl ketones, benzylamines, and aromatic amides from aromatic amines.
subject: Chemistry

question: What product is obtained when benzenediazonium chloride is treated with $\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}$, followed by acid-catalyzed hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+, \Delta$)?
explanation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+, \Delta} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$.
subject: Chemistry

question: What product is obtained when benzonitrile (formed by Sandmeyer cyanation) is reduced with $\text{LiAlH}_4$ or catalytic hydrogenation?
explanation: Reduction of the cyano group adds four hydrogen atoms across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN} + 4[\text{H}] \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.
subject: Chemistry

question: Which of the following describes the oxidation state transformation of copper during the first step of the Sandmeyer mechanism?
options: Copper(I) is reduced to metallic Copper(0)
Copper(I) is oxidized to Copper(II) as it transfers an electron to the diazonium cation
Copper remains in the $+3$ oxidation state throughout
explanation: $\text{Cu}^\text{I} + \text{Ar-N}_2^+ \rightarrow \text{Cu}^\text{II} + \text{Ar}^\bullet + \text{N}_2$. Copper acts as a one-electron donor.
subject: Chemistry

question: Which of the following describes the second step of the Sandmeyer catalytic cycle?
options: The aryl radical combines with water to form phenol
The aryl radical attacks the benzene ring of another molecule
The aryl radical ($\text{Ar}^\bullet$) abstracts a halogen atom from $\text{Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}_2$, yielding the aryl halide ($\text{Ar-X}$) and regenerating the copper(I) catalyst
Copper is converted permanently to insoluble copper sulfide
explanation: $\text{Ar}^\bullet + [\text{X-Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}] \rightarrow \text{Ar-X} + \text{Cu}^\text{I}\text{X}$. This ligand-transfer step regenerates $\text{Cu}^\text{I}$.
subject: Chemistry

question: What spectroscopic technique has been used to detect the transient aryl radical intermediates in the Sandmeyer reaction?
options: Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) spectroscopy / Radical trapping with TEMPO
explanation: Radical scavengers (like TEMPO or acrylonitrile) trap the aryl radical, confirming the single-electron transfer free-radical pathway.
subject: Chemistry

question: Can electron-withdrawing groups (such as $-\text{NO}_2$ or $-\text{CF}_3$) on the aromatic ring tolerate the Sandmeyer reaction?
options: Yes, the Sandmeyer reaction proceeds smoothly with aromatic rings bearing electron-withdrawing or electron-donating groups
No, electron-withdrawing groups cause spontaneous explosion of the catalyst
No, nitro groups turn into hydroxyl groups
Electron-withdrawing groups convert the diazonium salt into an alkane
explanation: The Sandmeyer reaction has broad functional group tolerance; both electron-deficient and electron-rich arenediazonium salts undergo efficient substitution.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the product when $p$-nitrobenzenediazonium chloride is treated with $\text{CuBr} / \text{HBr}$?
explanation: The diazonium group at the 1-position is selectively replaced by bromine, leaving the 4-nitro substituent intact: $p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{N}_2^+ + \text{CuBr} \rightarrow p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{Br} + \text{N}_2$.
subject: Chemistry

question: How is chlorobenzene synthesized commercially in the laboratory starting from nitrobenzene?
explanation: This classic 3-step sequence (Reduction $\rightarrow$ Diazotization $\rightarrow$ Sandmeyer) is the textbook route from nitroarenes to haloarenes.
subject: Chemistry

question: What happens if water is present and the Sandmeyer mixture is warmed without sufficient cuprous halide?
options: Phenol is formed as a major byproduct due to competitive heterolytic or homolytic solvolysis by water
explanation: In the absence of sufficient halide/copper catalyst, diazonium ions hydrolyze upon warming: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ar-OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{H}^+$.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the primary advantage of the Sandmeyer reaction over direct halogenation for introducing bromine into benzoic acid at the meta position?
options: Direct bromination of benzoic acid requires harsh forcing conditions and gives low yields, whereas converting $m$-nitrobenzoic acid via reduction, diazotization, and Sandmeyer reaction gives clean $m$-bromobenzoic acid
Direct bromination gives only ortho-bromobenzoic acid
explanation: The Sandmeyer approach provides high isomeric purity and mild reaction conditions for substituted aryl halides.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the formula of cuprous chloride used in the Sandmeyer reaction?
explanation: Cuprous chloride has copper in the $+1$ oxidation state and exists as a tetrahedral cluster/dimer $\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2$ in the crystalline and solution state.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why is $\text{HCl}$ used in conjunction with $\text{CuCl}$ in the Sandmeyer chlorination?
options: $\text{CuCl}$ is virtually insoluble in pure water; concentrated $\text{HCl}$ dissolves it by forming soluble chlorocuprate(I) complex ions such as $[\text{CuCl}_2]^-$ and $[\text{CuCl}_3]^{2-}$
explanation: Cuprous chloride dissolves readily in concentrated $\text{HCl}$ via complex ion formation: $\text{CuCl} + \text{Cl}^- \rightleftharpoons [\text{CuCl}_2]^-$, ensuring a homogeneous and active catalytic species.
subject: Chemistry

question: In the preparation of $o$-bromotoluene from $o$-toluidine via the Sandmeyer reaction, what are the sequential reagents?
explanation: $o$-Toluidine is diazotized with nitrous acid and hydrobromic acid at ice-cold temperature, followed by addition of cuprous bromide in hydrobromic acid to yield $o$-bromotoluene.
subject: Chemistry

question: Which of the following haloarenes CANNOT be prepared by the Sandmeyer reaction?
options: None; all three can be prepared
explanation: Fluorobenzene cannot be prepared by the Sandmeyer reaction; it is synthesized by the Balz-Schiemann reaction.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the oxidation state of copper in $\text{CuCN}$?
explanation: Copper is in the cuprous state ($	ext{Cu}^+$) with a $\text{d}^{10}$ electron configuration.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why is the Sandmeyer reaction categorized as an organometallic radical reaction?
options: Because a transition metal ($\text{Cu}^\text{I}$) mediates the formation and transfer of free radical intermediates without generating free carbanions or benzyne
Because copper metal is melted into liquid
explanation: The discovery of copper-catalyzed radical generation from diazonium salts helped pioneer modern transition-metal-catalyzed cross-coupling and radical chemistry.
subject: Chemistry

question: How does the reactivity of arenediazonium salts in the Sandmeyer reaction compare to that of aliphatic diazonium salts?
options: Aliphatic diazonium salts give higher yields than aromatic ones
Both are stable at room temperature for months
Arenediazonium salts are sufficiently stable at $0-5^\circ\text{C}$ to participate in the Sandmeyer reaction, whereas aliphatic diazonium salts decompose uncontrollably within picoseconds
explanation: Aliphatic diazonium ions undergo instantaneous loss of $\text{N}_2$ to yield carbocation rearrangements and mixtures; only aromatic diazonium salts are stable enough for the Sandmeyer reaction.
subject: Chemistry

question: What happens if a Sandmeyer chlorination is carried out using $\text{CuSO}_4 + \text{NaCl}$ without a reducing agent?
options: Reaction fails or gives low yields because $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (copper(II)) cannot initiate the single-electron transfer reduction of the diazonium cation
explanation: The active catalyst is $\text{Cu}^\text{I}$, not $\text{Cu}^\text{II}$. If copper(II) sulfate is used, it must first be reduced to $\text{Cu}^\text{I}$ with sodium sulfite or copper turnings.
subject: Chemistry

question: What reagent mixture is commonly used to freshly prepare cuprous chloride solution in the laboratory?
explanation: Copper(II) is reduced to copper(I) by sulfite: $2\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^- + \text{SO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{CuCl}\downarrow + \text{SO}_4^{2-} + 2\text{H}^+$.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the product when $p$-toluidine undergoes diazotization followed by treatment with $\text{CuCN} / \text{KCN}$?
explanation: The diazonium group of $p$-methylbenzenediazonium chloride is replaced by $-\text{CN}$, producing $p$-tolunitrile.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the byproduct gas released when arenediazonium chloride is warmed with copper powder and $\text{HCl}$ in the Gattermann reaction?
explanation: Both Sandmeyer and Gattermann reactions expel dinitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$) quantitatively as the diazonium group is replaced.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why is potassium iodide ($\text{KI}$) simply added to the cold diazonium solution without any copper salt to prepare iodobenzene?
options: Because $\text{I}^-$ is easily oxidized to $\text{I}^\bullet$ by $[\text{Ar-N}_2]^+$, generating the aryl radical and iodine atoms that combine to give $\text{Ar-I}$
Because iodine boils at low temperatures
Because potassium forms an explosive alloy with copper
Because diazonium iodide is completely insoluble
explanation: The reduction potential of diazonium cation ($E^\circ \approx +0.45\text{ V}$) is high enough to be directly reduced by iodide ($E^\circ(\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-) = +0.54\text{ V}$), rendering copper catalyst unnecessary.
subject: Chemistry

question: Which of the following compounds can be synthesized from aniline via a Sandmeyer reaction followed by alkaline hydrolysis?
options: Phenol (if hydrolyzed directly) or Benzoic acid (if converted to benzonitrile then hydrolyzed)
explanation: Sequence: Aniline $\rightarrow$ Benzenediazonium salt $\xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}}$ Benzonitrile $\xrightarrow{\text{OH}^-, \Delta, \text{H}^+}$ Benzoic acid.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the effect of replacing $\text{CuCl}$ with $\text{CuBr}$ in the Sandmeyer reaction?
options: A nitro group is introduced instead
The reaction introduces a bromine atom instead of a chlorine atom onto the aromatic ring
explanation: The nature of the halogen transferred to the aryl radical depends entirely on the cuprous halide employed ($\text{CuCl} \rightarrow \text{Ar-Cl}$; $\text{CuBr} \rightarrow \text{Ar-Br}$).
subject: Chemistry

question: When benzenediazonium chloride is treated with $\text{CuCl} / \text{HCl}$ in the presence of an alkene (such as styrene or acrylic acid), what reaction occurs instead?
options: Meerwein Arylation (radical addition of the aryl group and chlorine across the double bond of the alkene)
explanation: In the presence of alkenes, the copper-generated aryl radical attacks the $\text{C=C}$ double bond, followed by chlorine transfer from $\text{CuCl}_2$; this is known as the Meerwein arylation.
subject: Chemistry

question: Why does the Sandmeyer reaction require an acidic environment for chlorination and bromination?
options: Acid prevents the decomposition of the arenediazonium salt into diazotate or phenol and stabilizes the chlorocuprate(I) species
Acid turns the benzene ring into a gas
Acid causes precipitation of metallic copper
explanation: At neutral or basic pH, diazonium ions hydrolyze or convert to unreactive diazotates, and cuprous halides precipitate as unreactive copper(I) oxide ($\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$).
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the thermal stability of dry benzenediazonium chloride?
options: It is violently explosive when dry and must never be isolated; it is always handled in cold aqueous solution
It is a liquid that freezes at $100^\circ\text{C}$
explanation: Dry arenediazonium halides are shock- and heat-sensitive primary explosives. Sandmeyer reactions are always carried out in situ without isolating the dry salt.
subject: Chemistry

question: In the synthesis of saccharin (an artificial sweetener), which reaction is used to convert 2-aminobenzoic acid methyl ester into the corresponding sulfonyl chloride via diazotization?
options: A modified Sandmeyer-type sulfochlorination using $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{CuCl}_2$ (Meerwein-Sandmeyer sulfochlorination)
explanation: Treatment of diazonium salts with $\text{SO}_2$ in the presence of $\text{CuCl}$ yields arylsulfonyl chlorides ($\text{Ar-SO}_2\text{Cl}$), a valuable variant of the Sandmeyer reaction.
subject: Chemistry

question: What happens when an arenediazonium salt is treated with $\text{Cu(NO}_2)_2$ in the presence of $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ or $\text{Cu}$ powder?
options: The ring expands into a seven-membered tropylium cation
The diazonium group is replaced by a nitro group ($-\text{NO}_2$), yielding a nitroarene
explanation: A modified Sandmeyer reaction using sodium nitrite and cuprous oxide introduces a nitro group, useful for synthesizing nitro compounds inaccessible by direct nitration.
subject: Chemistry

question: What is the general yield and synthetic importance of the Sandmeyer reaction in modern pharmaceutical chemistry?
options: Yields typically exceed $70-85\%$; it is an indispensable tool for introducing halogen and nitrile handles for subsequent transition-metal-catalyzed cross-couplings (Suzuki, Heck, Buchwald)
Yields are less than $1\%$, making it obsolete
It is only used for making inorganic minerals
It converts all pharmaceuticals into toxic cyanide
explanation: The aryl halides and benzonitriles produced by the Sandmeyer reaction are fundamental building blocks for carbon-carbon and carbon-heteroatom bond construction in medicinal chemistry.
subject: Chemistry
